H1.text: Lift a bucket of water. Push a cupboard across the room. Pull a cart of books.

H2.text: In daily life, we call all three hard work. But physics is stricter.

H3.text: Diya lifts her eight kilogram bag onto a shelf, one metre up. Then she carries it ten metres down the corridor.

H4.text: Her arms ache both times. But physics says she did work on the bag only once. Which time?

H5.text: One small formula will tell us.

P1.text: So what is work in physics?

P2.text: Work is done when a force moves something. A force must act, and the thing must move.

P3.text: Push a wall all day. It does not move. So you do no work on it, however tired you feel.

P4.text: And only the part of the force along the motion counts. That is the shadow from the last episode.

P5.text: So work is force, times displacement, times cos theta.

S1.text: Let's measure work live. Diya drags a box of books with a rope. She pulls with fifty newtons.

S2.text: First, the rope is flat, so theta is zero. Watch the work meter.

S3.text: One metre, fifty joules. Two metres, one hundred. Four metres, two hundred joules.

S4.text: Now she pulls at sixty degrees. The same fifty newtons, the same four metres.

S5.text: This time the meter stops at one hundred joules. Only half her pull is along the floor.

S7.text: F is along the rope. Its forward part is F cos theta, twenty five newtons. The box moves along d.

S8.text: On the graph, work grows in a straight line. The flat rope gives the steeper line.

D1.text: Now the formula, one small step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Work is the forward part of the force, times the displacement. W equals F cos theta, times d.

D3.text: Step two. That is exactly a dot product. W equals F dot d.

D4.text: Step three. Force and displacement are vectors, but their dot product is a number. So work is a scalar. A size, no direction.

D5.text: Step four. One newton, moving something one metre along it, does one joule of work. Its dimensions are M L squared T to the minus two.

T1.text: Remember this. Work needs a force and a displacement. Only the part of the force along the motion counts.

C1.text: Now, back to Diya's bag. Side by side.

C2.text: Lifting. Her force is up, the bag moves up, so theta is zero. Work is m g h. Eight, times nine point eight, times one, about seventy eight joules.

C3.text: Carrying. Her hand still pushes up, but the bag moves sideways. Theta is ninety degrees, and cos ninety is zero. So her work on the bag is zero.

C4.text: Now you try. Diya holds the bag still, for five minutes. Her arms ache. How much work does she do on the bag? Pause and think.

C5.text: Zero! The bag does not move, so d is zero. Her muscles use energy inside her body, but she does no work on the bag.

R1.text: So how do you know if a force does work? Check three links.

R2.text: Is there a force? Did the object move? Is some of the force along the motion?

R3.text: Pushing a wall. Force, yes. Moved, no. No work.

R4.text: Carrying the bag sideways. Force, yes. Moved, yes. Along the motion, no. No work.

R5.text: Dragging the box. Yes, yes, and yes. Work is done.

W2.text: A force of six i plus two j newtons moves a box from the point one, two, to the point five, five, in metres. Find the work done.

W3.text: First, the displacement. Final minus initial. Five minus one is four, five minus two is three. So d is four i plus three j.

W4.text: Now, W equals F dot d. Six times four is twenty four. Two times three is six.

W5.text: Add them. The work done is thirty joules.

X2.text: A rope makes thirty degrees with the vertical. Many students write W equals F d cos thirty.

X3.text: But theta is measured from the motion. The box moves along the floor, so theta is sixty degrees. W equals F d cos sixty.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Work as F dot d with vectors, a pull at an angle, and the unit and dimensions of work.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A ten kilogram box is pulled five metres at a steady speed on a rough floor, by a rope at thirty seven degrees above the floor. Mu is point seven five and g is ten. Cos thirty seven is point eight, sine thirty seven is point six. Find the work done by the rope. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Two hundred and forty joules.

A2.text: Steady speed, so the forces balance. F cos theta equals friction.

A3.text: Friction is mu N, and N is m g minus F sin theta.

A4.text: So point eight F equals point seven five, times one hundred minus point six F. F is sixty newtons.

A5.text: The forward part is forty eight newtons. Times five metres, that is two hundred and forty joules.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does pushing a wall all day do no work on it?

Y3.text: Two. Why is work a scalar, though force and displacement are vectors?

Y4.text: Three. What is one joule, in your own words?

N1.text: Next time: brakes, a ceiling fan, and books carried down a corridor. Positive work, negative work, and no work at all. We find out in positive, negative and zero work.
